CANARY: the canary in the coal mine

Source: vignettes/canary.Rmd
canary.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

Gould and Wang (2017) use external information about the event rate in patients not receiving the test product to judge whether the blinded total event count \(X\) is higher than expected. With \(N\) subjects, \(N_d = \mathrm{round}(k N / (k + 1))\) on study drug and \(N_c = N - N_d\) on control (the expected arm sizes), \(X\) is the sum of \(\mathrm{Binomial}(N_d, p_d)\) and \(\mathrm{Binomial}(N_c, p_c)\) counts. The control probability has an informative Beta prior, and the metric of the difference (the ratio \(R = p_d / p_c\), the difference, or the odds ratio) has a diffuse prior: for the ratio, a lognormal distribution with mean 1 and probability 0.95 between 0.1 and 10, truncated to \(R \le 1 / p_c\). For large trials and rare events, a Poisson likelihood with a Gamma prior of the control rate is used instead. canary_post() integrates the two-dimensional posterior (one-dimensional for the Poisson likelihood) numerically.

canary_post(y = 12, n = 100, k = 1, prior_c = c(1, 49))
#> Model: CANARY 
#> Tested quantity: ratio R = p_d / p_c of the event probabilities
#> P(R > 1 | data) = 0.8417
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of R: mean 3.156, median 2.389, 95% interval (0.3521, 10.53)
canary_post(y = 12, n = 100, k = 1, prior_c = c(1, 49),
            metric = "difference")
#> Model: CANARY 
#> Tested quantity: difference D = p_d - p_c of the event probabilities
#> P(D > 0 | data) = 0.9956
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): yes
#> Posterior of D: mean 0.2108, median 0.2113, 95% interval (0.06536, 0.3504)

Decision rules and their operating characteristics

Over the range of counts that matters for monitoring, the posterior probability increases with the event count, so a rule “\(P(R > R_\mathrm{crit} \mid X) > \gamma_\mathrm{crit}\)” is equivalent to \(X \ge X_\mathrm{crit}\). (For counts close to \(N\), both event probabilities must be close to 1, and the probability of a large ratio falls again; signal_count() therefore searches upward from 0.) signal_count() finds \(X_\mathrm{crit}\) for each sample size (the control charts of Figure 2), and count_oc() gives the exact probability of reaching it under true event rates (Figure 3 and Table V).

sc <- signal_count(n = c(100, 200, 500), method = "canary",
                   prior_c = c(20, 980), crit = 2, cutoff = 0.8)
sc
#>     n y_crit      prob prob_below
#> 1 100      8 0.8516000  0.7357937
#> 2 200     12 0.8264072  0.7406849
#> 3 500     24 0.8159702  0.7685790
count_oc(sc$y_crit, sc$n, rate_c = 0.02, rate_d = 0.08)
#> [1] 0.1259040 0.2990768 0.6115370

Reproduction of Gould and Wang (2017)

inst/reproduce/reproduce_Gould2017.R compares

  • the 24 prior parameters of Table I, from elicit_prior(): 24 PASS;
  • the 24 critical counts of Table III (binomial likelihood): 11 PASS and 13 EXPLAINED;
  • the 4 critical counts of Table V (Poisson likelihood): 0 PASS and 4 EXPLAINED;
  • the 36 probabilities of Table V, from count_oc(): 36 PASS.

The published critical counts were computed by the authors’ R code on fixed grids. A transcription of the code, kept outside the package because the code has no stated license, reproduces 28 of the 28 published counts (inst/validation/python/ref_gould2017_author_grid.csv); the differences from the exact counts of bssd come from the grids (100 values of \(R\) in \((0, 10)\), with the threshold 2 evaluated at the grid point 1.98, for the binomial model; a coarse grid of the expected control count for the Poisson model). The binomial counts of Table III were computed with the lognormal prior between 0.1 and 8, the default of the authors’ code, which is used here as well.

Numerical integration

Against independent Python computations on dense grids split exactly at the thresholds, the largest absolute difference of the 24 compared quantities (four data sets with the ratio, the difference, the odds ratio and the Poisson likelihood) is 6.3e-07. For the Poisson likelihood, MCMC in JAGS gives 0.2214 for \(P(R > 2 \mid X)\) against 0.2213 from bssd (PASS).

References

Gould, A. L. and Wang, W. B. (2017). Monitoring potential adverse event rate differences using data from blinded trials: the canary in the coal mine. Statistics in Medicine, 36(1), 92–104. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.7129
